Easy Visa¶

Context¶

Business communities in the United States are facing high demand for human resources, but one of the constant challenges is identifying and attracting the right talent, which is perhaps the most important element in remaining competitive. Companies in the United States look for hard-working, talented, and qualified individuals both locally as well as abroad. The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of the US permits foreign workers to come to the United States to work on either a temporary or permanent basis. The act also protects US workers against adverse impacts on their wages or working conditions by ensuring US employers' compliance with statutory requirements when they hire foreign workers to fill workforce shortages. The immigration programs are administered by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC). OFLC processes job certification applications for employers seeking to bring foreign workers into the United States and grants certifications in those cases where employers can demonstrate that there are not sufficient US workers available to perform the work at wages that meet or exceed the wage paid for the occupation in the area of intended employment.

Objective¶

In FY 2016, the OFLC processed 775,979 employer applications for 1,699,957 positions for temporary and permanent labor certifications. This was a nine percent increase in the overall number of processed applications from the previous year. The process of reviewing every case is becoming a tedious task as the number of applicants is increasing every year. The increasing number of applicants every year calls for a Machine Learning based solution that can help in shortlisting the candidates having higher chances of VISA approval. OFLC has hired the firm EasyVisa for data-driven solutions. You as a data scientist at EasyVisa have to analyze the data provided and, with the help of a classification model:

  1. Facilitate the process of visa approvals.
  2. Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of the employee and the employer. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

Column Name Dexcription
case_id ID of each visa application
continent Information of continent of the employee
education_of_employee Information of education of the employee
has_job_experience Does the employee has any job experience? Y= Yes; N = No
requires_job_training Does the employee require any job training? Y = Yes; N = No
no_of_employees Number of employees in the employer's company
yr_of_estab Year in which the employer's company was established
region_of_employment Information of foreign worker's intended region of employment in the US.
prevailing_wage Average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment. The purpose of the prevailing wage is to ensure that the foreign worker is not underpaid compared to other workers offering the same or similar service in the same area of employment.
unit_of_wage Unit of prevailing wage. Values include Hourly, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly.
full_time_position Is the position of work full-time?
Y = Full-Time Position
N = Part-Time Position
case_status Flag indicating if the Visa was certified or denied

🔎 Observations:

  • continent: The majority of cases originate from Asia (66%), followed by Europe (14.6%) and North America (12.9%). Oceania and Africa have minimal representation.
  • education_of_employee: Most applicants have a Bachelor’s (40%) or Master’s degree (37.8%), with fewer High School (13.4%) and Doctorate (8.6%) holders.
  • has_job_experience: A slight majority (58%) have prior job experience, but a significant 42% do not.
  • requires_job_training: Only 11.6% require job training, meaning most applicants are already skilled.
  • region_of_employment: Employment is fairly distributed across regions, with Northeast (28.2%) and South (27.5%) leading, followed by West (25.8%) and Midwest (16.9%).
  • unit_of_wage: The majority (90.2%) are paid yearly, while hourly wages (8.5%) are the next most common. Weekly and monthly wages are rare.
  • full_time_position: Most positions are full-time (89.4%), while only 10.6% are part-time.
  • case_status: 66.8% of cases are certified, while 33.2% are denied, indicating a moderate rejection rate. Potential imbalance should be checked in modeling.

def univariate_analysis(data,col,cat=False, legend=False):
    sns.set_palette(['darkturquoise'])
    colors = ['lightcoral','lightsalmon','palegoldenrod','lightgreen','lightblue','lightcyan']

    if cat and legend:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

        # Countplot
        sns.countplot(data=data, x=col, ax=ax[0])
        ax[0].set_title(f'{col} Distribution (Countplot)')

        # Pie chart data
        value_counts = data[col].value_counts()
        sizes = value_counts.values
        labels = value_counts.index

        chart_colors = colors[:len(labels)]

        # Create the pie chart
        wedges, texts = ax[1].pie(
            sizes,
            labels=None,  # Do not display labels directly on the pie chart
            autopct=None,  # Show percentages on the wedges
            startangle=90,
            colors=chart_colors,
            wedgeprops={'edgecolor': 'white', 'linewidth': 2}
        )

        # Add a legend to the right of the pie chart
        ax[1].legend(
            wedges,  # Use the wedges as handles for the legend
            [f"{label}: {size / sum(sizes) * 100:.1f}%" for label, size in zip(labels, sizes)],  # Custom labels with percentages
            title="Continents",  # Title for the legend
            loc="center left",  # Position the legend to the right of the pie chart
            bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.5),  # Adjust position (x=1 places it outside the chart)
        )

        ax[1].set_title(f'{col} Distribution (Pie Chart)')

        plt.tight_layout()
        return
    elif cat and not legend:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize = (10,3));

        sns.countplot(data = data, x = col, ax = ax[0])
        ax[0].set_title(f'{col} Distribution (Countplot)');

        # Plotting Pie Chart
        value_counts = data[col].value_counts()
        sizes = value_counts.values 
        labels = value_counts.index 

        chart_colors = colors[:len(labels)]
        
        ax[1].pie(
            sizes,
            labels=labels,
            autopct='%1.1f%%', 
            startangle=90,       
            colors=chart_colors,
            wedgeprops={'edgecolor': 'white', 'linewidth': 2}
        );
        ax[1].set_title(f'{col} Distribution (Pie Chart)');
        return
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize = (10,3));

    sns.histplot(data = data, x = col, ax = ax[0], kde=True)
    ax[0].set_title(f'{col} Distribution (Histogram)');
    ax[0].axvline(data[col].mean(), c = 'r', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label=f'Mean: {data[col].mean():.2f}')
    ax[0].axvline(data[col].median(), c = 'y', linestyle='-', linewidth=2, label=f'Median: {data[col].median():.2f}')
    ax[0].legend(loc='upper right')

    sns.boxplot(data = data, x = col, ax = ax[1])
    ax[1].set_title(f'{col} Distribution (Boxplot)');

🔎 Observations:

  1. Skewed Distribution:

    • The histogram shows that the distribution of no_of_employees is highly right-skewed, with most companies having a relatively small number of employees.
    • A few companies have extremely high employee counts, creating long tails in the data.

  2. Mean vs Median:

    • The mean number of employees is 5,667.09, while the median is significantly lower at 2,109.
    • This indicates the presence of outliers (companies with very high employee counts) pulling the mean upward.

  3. Outliers:

    • The boxplot highlights numerous outliers, with employee counts going up to 600,000.
    • These outliers represent large organizations or companies with massive workforces.

  4. Majority of Cases:

    • Most companies have fewer than 10,000 employees, as seen from the concentration of values on the left side of the histogram.

🌟 Model Building - Bagging 🌟¶

Model Evaluation Criteria

A model can err in two ways:

  1. False Positive: The model predicts that a visa application will be approved, but in reality, it should have been rejected.
  2. False Negative: The model predicts that a visa application will be rejected, but in reality, it should have been approved.

Which Scenario is More Critical?

Both scenarios carry significant implications:

  • False Positive: If a visa is approved when it should have been denied, an unsuitable candidate might secure a job, potentially displacing a qualified U.S. citizen from that opportunity.

  • False Negative: If a visa is denied when it should have been approved, the U.S. economy might miss out on valuable talent that could contribute to growth and innovation.

Strategies to Minimize Errors

To mitigate these risks:

  • **F1 Score**: We will employ the F1 Score as our primary evaluation metric. A higher F1 Score indicates better performance in reducing both False Positives and False Negatives.

  • Balanced Class Weights: We will adjust the model to give equal importance to both classes, ensuring that the model does not favor one outcome over the other due to class imbalance.

In [49]:
def model_performance_classification(model, predicators, target):
    pred = model.predict(predicators)
    precision = precision_score(target,pred)
    recall = recall_score(target,pred)
    accuracy = accuracy_score(target,pred)
    f1 = f1_score(target,pred)

    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": accuracy, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

def plot_confusion_matrix(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    # Predict the target values using the provided model and predictors
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)

    # Compute the confusion matrix comparing the true target values with the predicted values
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)

    # Extract values from the confusion matrix
    tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()

    # Calculate total samples
    total = np.sum(cm)

    # Calculate percentages
    tp_percent = (tp / total) * 100
    tn_percent = (tn / total) * 100
    fp_percent = (fp / total) * 100
    fn_percent = (fn / total) * 100

    # Create labels for each cell in the confusion matrix with both count and percentage
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)    # reshaping to a matrix

    # Set the figure size for the plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))

    # Plot the confusion matrix as a heatmap with the labels
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")

    # Add a label to the y-axis
    plt.ylabel("True label")

    # Add a label to the x-axis
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

    # Add a title to the plot
    plt.title("Confusion Matrix for Model Performance on Test Data")

    # Print the results
    print("🔎 Observations:\n")
    print(f"1. True Positives (predicted=1, actual=1): {tp} ({tp_percent:.2f}%)")
    print(f"2. True Negatives (predicted=0, actual=0): {tn} ({tn_percent:.2f}%)")
    print(f"3. False Positives (predicted=1, actual=0): {fp} ({fp_percent:.2f}%)")
    print(f"4. False Negatives (predicted=0, actual=1): {fn} ({fn_percent:.2f}%)")

def build_model(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test):
    model.fit(X_train,y_train)

    # Evaluate model performance on train & test sets
    train_perf = model_performance_classification(model, X_train, y_train)
    test_perf = model_performance_classification(model, X_test, y_test)

    print("Train Performance:\n", train_perf)
    print('\n---------------------------------\n')
    print("Confusion Matrix for Model Performance on Test Data:\n")
    plot_confusion_matrix(model, X_test, y_test)
    print('\n---------------------------------\n')
    print("Test Performance:\n", test_perf)

    return train_perf, test_perf


def tune_model(params, skf, model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, scoring='f1', n_iter=30):
    """
    Performs hyperparameter tuning using RandomizedSearchCV, evaluates with cross-validation,
    and returns model performance on train & test sets.

    Parameters:
        params (dict): Hyperparameter grid for RandomizedSearchCV
        skf (KFold or StratifiedKFold): Cross-validation strategy
        model (sklearn model): Base model to be tuned
        X_train (pd.DataFrame): Training predictors
        y_train (pd.Series): Training target
        X_test (pd.DataFrame): Test predictors
        y_test (pd.Series): Test target
        scoring (str): Metric to optimize during RandomizedSearchCV (default: 'f1')
        n_iter (int): Number of iterations for RandomizedSearchCV (default: 30)

    Returns:
        dict: Contains best parameters, cross-validation scores, train & test performance
    """
    
    # Perform RandomizedSearchCV without refitting
    random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
        estimator=model, param_distributions=params, 
        n_iter=n_iter, cv=skf, scoring=scoring, 
        verbose=2, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42, refit=True
    )
    
    # Fit on training data
    random_search.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Get best hyperparameters
    best_params = random_search.best_params_
    print("Best Parameters:", best_params)
    print('\n---------------------------------\n')

    # Step 4: Compute cross-validation scores (using best model)
    cv_scores = cross_val_score(random_search, X_train, y_train, cv=skf, scoring=scoring, n_jobs=-1)
    print(f"Mean cross-validation {scoring} score: {cv_scores.mean()}")
    print('\n---------------------------------\n')
    
    # Evaluate model performance on train & test sets
    train_perf = model_performance_classification(random_search, X_train, y_train)
    test_perf = model_performance_classification(random_search, X_test, y_test)

    print("Train Performance:\n", train_perf)
    print('\n---------------------------------\n')
    print("Confusion Matrix for Model Performance on Test Data:\n")
    plot_confusion_matrix(random_search, X_test, y_test)
    print('\n---------------------------------\n')
    print("Test Performance:\n", test_perf)

    return {
        "best_model" : random_search,
        "best_params": best_params,
        "cv_scores": cv_scores,
        "train_performance": train_perf,
        "test_performance": test_perf
    }

📌 Model Performance Summary¶

We evaluated three models — Decision Tree, Bagging Classifier, and Random Forest — across the original, oversampled, and undersampled datasets. Below is a detailed analysis of their performance:

  1. Decision Tree

    • Shows signs of overfitting on all datasets.
    • Generalization is slightly better with the oversampled dataset, as it balances recall and precision more effectively.
    • Best F1 Performance is achieved with oversampling, making it a preferable choice.

  2. Bagging Classifier

    • More stable compared to the Decision Tree, reducing overfitting.
    • Generalizes best with the original dataset, maintaining strong recall and precision without excessive variance.
    • Best F1 Performance is also with the original dataset, making it the most reliable option.

  3. Random Forest

    • Consistently the strongest performer across all datasets.
    • Generalizes best with the original dataset, striking a balance between recall and precision.
    • Best F1 Performance is also observed with original dataset, reinforcing its robustness.

🏆 Selecting the Best Dataset for Each Model¶

✔ Decision Tree → Oversampled Data (Better generalization & F1 score)
✔ Bagging Classifier → Original Data (Strong balance & generalization)
✔ Random Forest → Original Data (Best F1 & most reliable)

🚀 Performance Analysis of Bagging Classifiers¶

Since our primary metric is the F1-score, let's evaluate each model accordingly.

1️⃣ Tuned Decision Tree Performance¶

  • The model has high recall, meaning it captures most positive cases.
  • However, precision is lower, indicating a higher number of false positives.
  • The F1 score on test data is close to the mean cross-validation F1 score, suggesting good generalization but lower overall performance compared to bagging models.

2️⃣ Tuned Bagging Classifier Performance¶

  • More balanced between precision and recall compared to the Decision Tree.
  • The F1 score on test data is close to the cross-validation mean, indicating strong generalization.
  • Performs better than the Decision Tree but slightly behind Random Forest in terms of overall classification power.

3️⃣ Tuned Random Forest Performance¶

  • Achieves the highest F1-score on training data, showing strong learning capacity.
  • Precision and recall are well-balanced, leading to strong classification performance.
  • The test F1 score aligns closely with its cross-validation mean, confirming strong generalization with minimal overfitting.
  • The highest accuracy and best overall F1-score make it the most effective model.

🏆 Best Model Selection¶

1️⃣ Random Forest – Best overall performance with slight overfitting but strong classification power.
2️⃣ Bagging Classifier – Close second, slightly behind in performance but better generalization.

If robust performance is the priority, Random Forest is the best choice. If lower overfitting and interpretability matter more, the Bagging Classifier is a strong alternative.

🏆 Performance Analysis of Boosting Models¶

1️⃣ Gradient Boosting performed the best overall:

  • Showed strong generalization, maintaining stable performance across train and test data.
  • The model was least affected by sampling strategies, making it a reliable choice.

2️⃣ XGBoost had the best train performance but lower test performance:

  • Exhibited signs of overfitting, performing significantly better on training data than test data.
  • Oversampling improved its stability slightly, but it still lagged behind Gradient Boosting in test performance.

3️⃣ AdaBoost showed balanced but slightly lower performance:

  • Maintained consistent results across different sampling techniques.
  • Performed best on Oversampled Data, making it a viable option for handling class imbalance.

🚀 Performance Evaluation of Tuned Boosting Models¶

1️⃣ Tuned AdaBoost Performance¶

  • The model has high recall but lower precision, leading to more false positives.
  • The F1 score on test data is very close to the cross-validation F1 score, confirming good generalization but lower overall performance than other boosting models.
  • Slight underfitting, making it stable but less optimal.

2️⃣ Tuned Gradient Boosting Performance¶

  • Well-balanced precision and recall, contributing to strong classification performance.
  • The F1 score on test data closely matches the cross-validation F1 score, suggesting excellent generalization.
  • Performs better than AdaBoost and slightly better than XGBoost in terms of overall stability.

3️⃣ Tuned XGBoost Performance¶

  • Has the highest training F1-score but a slightly lower test F1-score compared to Gradient Boosting.
  • The cross-validation F1 score is slightly lower than that of Gradient Boosting, indicating slightly higher overfitting.
  • Still a strong contender due to its competitive performance.

📌 Final Boosting Model Selection¶

✅ Gradient Boosting is the best choice due to its strong generalization and balanced metrics.
✅ XGBoost is a close second, offering slightly better training performance but with a minor overfitting risk.

🌟 Final Model Selection 🌟¶

🚀 Comparison of Model Performance¶

We compare the models based on accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score, with a primary focus on F1-score to balance precision and recall. Additionally, we consider the mean cross-validation F1-score to assess generalization.

📊 1️⃣ Accuracy Comparison¶

🔎 Observations:

  • Random Forest has the highest training accuracy but shows a drop in test accuracy, suggesting overfitting.
  • Gradient Boosting and XGBoost maintain a strong balance between train and test accuracy.
  • Decision Tree and AdaBoost have similar accuracy, but their overall performance is weaker.

🎯 2️⃣ Recall Comparison (Higher is Better for Sensitivity)¶

🔎 Observations:

  • Decision Tree and AdaBoost have the highest recall, but this comes at the cost of lower precision.
  • Random Forest also maintains high recall while slightly improving precision, making it a strong contender.
  • Bagging, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost show more balanced recall and precision trade-offs.

✅ 3️⃣ Precision Comparison (Higher is Better for Reducing False Positives)¶

🔎 Observations:

  • Random Forest has the highest training precision, but XGBoost and Gradient Boosting perform better on test data.
  • Bagging Classifier has lower precision than Random Forest but performs slightly better than AdaBoost and Decision Tree.
  • Boosting methods (Gradient Boosting and XGBoost) offer strong precision without excessive overfitting.

📈 4️⃣ F1-Score Comparison (Primary Metric for Evaluation)¶

Mean Cross-Validation F1-Scores¶

Model CV F1-Score
Decision Tree 0.7959
Bagging Classifier 0.8180
Random Forest 0.8251
AdaBoost 0.7974
Gradient Boosting 0.8244
XGBoost 0.8188

🔎 Observations:

  • Gradient Boosting has the highest test F1-score, making it the most balanced model.
  • Random Forest has the highest cross-validation F1-score, but it also overfits more than Gradient Boosting.
  • XGBoost and Gradient Boosting are close competitors, but Gradient Boosting generalizes slightly better.
  • Bagging Classifier performs well and generalizes better than Decision Tree and AdaBoost.

🏆 Final Model Selection¶

✅ Best Overall Model: Gradient Boosting

  • Achieves the best balance between precision and recall.
  • Minimal overfitting compared to Random Forest and XGBoost.
  • Consistently strong across train, test, and cross-validation scores.

📌 Alternative Choices:

  • XGBoost: Strong performer, slightly more overfitting than Gradient Boosting.
  • Random Forest: Highest cross-validation score but more prone to overfitting.
  • Bagging Classifier: A more stable option than Decision Tree but slightly weaker than boosting models.

Final Recommendation: Use Gradient Boosting as the primary mode. 🚀

🌟 Actionable Insights & Recommendations 🌟¶

Actionable Insights¶

Based on the feature importance analysis from the Gradient Boosting model, here are the key insights:

  1. Education Levels:

    • The most critical factor influencing visa approval is the applicant's education level.
    • Applicants with High School education have the highest impact, followed by those with Master's and Doctorate degrees.

  2. Job Experience:

    • Having prior job experience (has_job_experience_Y) is a significant factor in determining visa approval likelihood.

  3. Prevailing Wage:

    • Higher prevailing wages are strongly associated with increased chances of visa approval.

  4. Regional Trends:

    • Employment regions such as the Midwest and South show greater importance in determining visa outcomes compared to others.
    • The Northeast region has relatively less influence on approvals.

  5. Continental Influence:

    • Applicants from continents like Europe and North America have a higher impact on approvals, while other regions (e.g., Asia, South America) are less influential.

  6. Full-Time Positions and Other Factors:

    • While full-time positions (full_time_position_Y) have some impact, they are less critical compared to education, experience, and wages.
    • Features like unit_of_wage_Year also play a role but are secondary in importance.

Recommendations¶

  1. Enhance Education-Based Hiring Strategies:

    • Employers should prioritize hiring candidates with higher education levels (e.g., Master's or Doctorate degrees) for specialized roles.
    • Offer skill development programs for candidates with only High School education to improve their employability.

  2. Prioritize Experienced Candidates:

    • Focus on hiring candidates with relevant job experience for roles requiring immediate expertise.
    • For less experienced candidates, create internship or training programs to build their skills.

  3. Offer Competitive Wages:

    • Employers should ensure that wage offerings align with or exceed market standards to attract skilled talent and improve visa approval rates.
    • Conduct regular wage benchmarking to stay competitive.

  4. Leverage Regional Trends:

    • Expand operations or hiring efforts in regions like the Midwest and South, which show favorable employment trends.
    • Investigate challenges in regions like the Northeast and address any barriers to approvals.

  5. Focus on Continental Support:

    • Provide targeted support for applicants from continents like Asia and South America, where visa approvals may face challenges (e.g., documentation issues or insufficient qualifications).

  6. Streamline Full-Time Roles:

    • Encourage full-time positions for roles requiring long-term commitment while maintaining flexibility for part-time opportunities where applicable.

Conclusion and Business Recommendations¶

  1. Model Selection:
    The Gradient Boosting model was chosen as it provides reliable predictions with balanced precision, recall, and F1-score on test data.

  2. Key Factors Influencing Approvals:
    Education level, job experience, prevailing wages, regional trends, and continental influences are critical drivers of visa approvals.

  3. Business Growth Strategies:

    • Focus on hiring highly educated and experienced candidates while offering competitive wages to attract top talent.
    • Expand operations in regions with favorable employment trends (e.g., Midwest, South) while addressing challenges in regions like the Northeast.
    • Provide targeted support for applicants from continents like Asia and South America to improve their success rates.
    • Invest in training programs for less experienced applicants to build a skilled workforce.
